title: Agriculture relies on fossil fuels. It’s costing us.
gist: The Iran conflict has driven natural gas and fertilizer prices to near-2022 highs by choking Strait of Hormuz trade and damaging ammonia plants, with CoBank forecasting elevated prices through at least 2028; microbial fertilizer startups Pivot Bio and Switch Bioworks are pitching gas-price-immune alternatives but can only substitute a minority of synthetic fertilizer today.

insights.claim: Natural gas functions as both the energy source and the core chemical feedstock for ammonia production, which tightly couples fertilizer prices to natural-gas price swings in a way most industries don't experience.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Fertilizer producers and ag-input investors should treat natural gas futures as a leading indicator for fertilizer margins and pricing, not just an input-cost line item.

insights.claim: The price of urea, the most commonly applied fertilizer, climbed above $850 per metric ton in April 2026, about 80% higher than pre-conflict levels and the highest level since the 2022 spike caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: An 80% urea spike is a concrete magnitude for modeling farm input-cost inflation and downstream food-price pass-through.

insights.claim: About one-third of global seaborne fertilizer trade passes through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed to commercial traffic because of the Iran conflict.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A structural chokepoint closure of this scale signals the fertilizer supply shock is a trade-logistics problem, not just a commodity-price problem, and won't resolve purely on gas prices easing.

insights.claim: The World Bank has warned that fertilizer access could worsen for some of the poorest countries as a result of the Strait of Hormuz closure.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Points to a food-security and social-stability risk concentrated in import-dependent developing economies, relevant for EM sovereign and ag-commodity risk assessments.

insights.claim: Fertilizer production accounts for about 2% of global greenhouse-gas emissions, an embedded climate cost layered on top of the current price volatility.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Gives a hard baseline for sizing the decarbonization opportunity available to non-fossil fertilizer alternatives.

insights.claim: The US largely meets its nitrogen fertilizer demand with domestic production but still imports some volume from the Persian Gulf, leaving it partially, not fully, insulated from the conflict's price effects.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: US farmers face milder but still real cost exposure versus fully import-dependent countries, a relevant nuance for domestic ag-input cost forecasts.

themes.theme: Structural damage extends the crisis beyond a price spike

insights.claim: CoBank, one of the largest agriculture-industry banks in the US, forecasts that some fertilizer prices could remain elevated through at least 2028.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A multi-year elevated-price forecast from a specialist ag lender is a signal for underwriting farm profitability and ag-input demand models out to 2028, not just through the current news cycle.

insights.claim: War damage to fertilizer production capacity is structural: 31 ammonia plants in the Middle East have been affected or shut down by the conflict, on top of 20 ammonia plants already damaged in Russia in recent years, removing roughly 51 plants' worth of capacity from the global system.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Physical plant destruction implies a supply-side recovery measured in years and capital spending, explaining why forecasters expect price relief to lag well behind any ceasefire.

insights.claim: Because farmers operate on paper-thin margins, sustained fertilizer price spikes are an existential cost pressure rather than a manageable inconvenience.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Thin farm margins mean input-cost inflation converts quickly into farm bankruptcies or planting reductions, a leading indicator for future crop-supply tightness.
insights.quote: The fertilizer price spikes, and because farmers have paper-thin margins, this is a real problem.

insights.claim: Farmers are facing compounding cost pressure this year from both volatile fertilizer prices and wild diesel prices simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Stacked energy-linked input costs (fertilizer plus fuel) compress farm margins from two directions at once, amplifying the food-price transmission mechanism.

themes.theme: Microbial fertilizer as a hedge, not yet a replacement

insights.claim: Pivot Bio markets genetically edited microbe fertilizer as cost-competitive with chemical fertilizer today and structurally insulated from gas-price spikes because it uses no natural-gas input; its CTO describes the current conventional supply chain as unusually volatile.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A fertilizer input with a cost structure decoupled from natural gas is a direct hedge against future geopolitical gas shocks, worth tracking as a competitive threat to incumbent nitrogen fertilizer producers.
insights.quote: There’s just this out-of-control supply chain that’s a lot more volatile than it’s ever been.

insights.claim: When the Iran war began, Pivot Bio raised its planned production volume, cut prices, and let farmers lock in prices for three years, moving opportunistically to capture demand from buyers spooked by conventional fertilizer volatility.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A three-year price lock is a concrete go-to-market tactic that could accelerate customer switching away from chemical fertilizer during periods of geopolitical stress.

insights.claim: Pivot Bio's products can replace only about 25% of synthetic fertilizer today depending on crop and conditions, with a company roadmap targeting 40% to 50% substitution over time.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Caps near-term expectations: microbial fertilizer is a partial hedge and margin play for now, not an imminent wholesale disruption of the incumbent nitrogen fertilizer industry.

insights.claim: Switch Bioworks is a second company, alongside Pivot Bio, developing advanced microbial fertilizers, indicating an emerging competitive category rather than a single-company story.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Multiple funded entrants suggest investor capital is already flowing into non-fossil nitrogen fertilizer, worth tracking as a distinct agtech subsector.

insights.claim: As long as fertilizer production remains dependent on fossil fuels, food prices will stay structurally tied to energy prices, according to Switch Bioworks' CEO, who argues the current system is unsustainable.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Frames the long-run investment case for alternative fertilizer as a bet on decoupling agricultural inflation from energy-market shocks.
insights.quote: We can’t keep doing it like this. There’s no way we can build a society where the basis of the food chain depends on fossil fuels.
